title: Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A student and a career advisor discuss how to evaluate a company’s stability before accepting a job offer.

script.en: I’ve got a final-round interview with a tech startup next week, but I’m a bit uneasy. The company launched a product two years ago, and I keep reading online that some customers are still waiting for their orders.

That’s a reasonable concern. Startups often struggle with logistics, but if the delays are widespread, it could signal deeper financial trouble. Have you checked whether the company has filed for any form of insolvency protection?
I don’t even know where to look. Their website is all marketing language, and the press releases only mention funding rounds from three years ago.

Try the government’s business registry. In the UK, for instance, you can search for a company’s filing history and see whether administrators have been appointed. It’s public information, and it often reveals more than the company’s own site.
That sounds useful. But suppose the company is financially healthy—how do I assess whether they treat their customers fairly? I don’t want to join a firm that ignores complaints.

Look at independent review platforms and social media groups. If customers repeatedly say they’ve received no response or refund, that’s a red flag. Also, during the interview, ask how the company handles after-sales support. The answer will tell you a lot about their priorities.
I’ll do that. One more thing: the role is in product management, and I’d be working closely with the founding team. Should I be worried if the founder has a reputation for being difficult?

It depends. A visionary founder can be inspiring, but if former employees describe a culture that revolves around one person’s whims, you might find it exhausting. Try to speak with current or former staff before you decide.
That’s helpful. I’ll reach out to a few people on LinkedIn and check the registry tonight. Thanks for the guidance.
You’re welcome. Remember, a job offer is a two-way street—you’re evaluating them as much as they’re evaluating you.

script.en: When a technology company collapses, the consequences often extend far beyond its employees and investors. Customers who have paid for products that never arrive, or who rely on software that may soon stop working, are often left with little recourse. This pattern has become familiar in the consumer electronics sector, where proprietary software and cloud services tie hardware to a company’s continued existence. Consider the case of a British music-technology firm that entered administration for the second time in its history. Although the company had once attracted celebrity investors and widespread praise, it had long faced complaints about communication. Customers reported orders delayed for months without explanation, and refunds were difficult to get. When the firm finally appointed administrators, it offered no public statement about outstanding orders. The problem is not merely financial. Many modern devices depend on companion apps and online accounts to function fully. If the company disappears, the hardware may continue to work for a while, but users fear that software support will eventually cease, rendering expensive equipment useless. This concern is particularly acute for products that cost hundreds or thousands of dollars. Legal protections for consumers vary by country. In some jurisdictions, buyers can file claims as creditors during insolvency proceedings, but the process is often slow and the recovery rate low. Consumer advocacy groups argue that companies should be needed to disclose their financial health more transparently and to ensure that software support outlives the hardware’s expected lifespan. For now, the lesson for buyers is caution. Before purchasing an expensive device that relies on proprietary software, consumers may want to research the company’s stability and read independent reviews. The collapse of a single firm can leave a community of users stranded, and the damage is not easily repaired.

sections.title: When Startups Fail, Customers Pay the Price
sections.passage: A technology company’s collapse rarely stays inside boardrooms and bankruptcy courts. Its effects often reach far beyond the money lost by investors and shareholders. When a firm sells hardware tied to its own software, customers can be left with few options. They may have paid for products or depend on continued support. But the devices they bought may need services the company can no longer maintain. This pattern has become more common in consumer electronics, and many devices depend on companion apps and cloud services to work fully. So the failure of one company can quickly affect a large group of users. A recent case in the British music-technology industry shows the problem clearly, and the company had once attracted celebrity investors and wide praise. It entered administration, the UK process for handling corporate insolvency, for the second time in its history. This left customers unsure about their orders and the future of their devices, and the firm had long faced complaints about communication. Yet it made no public statement about outstanding orders when administrators were appointed, and this deepened the frustration of buyers who had already paid. Customers who had paid hundreds or thousands of dollars for equipment reported delays of months or years. Many said they had received neither products nor refunds, despite repeated attempts to contact the company. The financial failure is only part of the story, however, and the technical consequences may prove even more damaging in the long run. Many modern instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps, and these tools help users connect, map sounds, and configure settings. Without continued updates, they may gradually stop working on newer operating systems, and the hardware may keep working for a while. But users fear that a lack of software support will eventually make their gear useless. Expensive equipment could become little more than obsolete hardware, and this concern is especially acute for expensive devices whose value depends on long-term usability. Buyers usually expect such products to remain functional for many years after purchase. Legal protections for consumers vary by jurisdiction, and the remedies available are often limited in practice. In some countries, buyers can file claims as creditors during insolvency proceedings. But the process is often slow and the recovery rate low, and most customers recover only a small fraction of what they paid. Consumer advocacy groups argue that companies should be required to disclose their financial health more transparently. They also say firms should ensure that software support outlives the hardware’s expected lifespan. This would prevent buyers from being left with devices that cannot be used as intended. For now, the lesson for buyers is caution.

long_sentences.en: “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.” Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise , tells WIRED.

You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.” In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace.
